idiom_name: function composed of static (internal-linkage) helper calls
implementation_notes: C has no member functions, so a macro method is an ordinary function whose body only calls other functions, with the steps declared static at file scope so they get internal linkage and stay invisible to the rest of the program (CERT rule DCL15-C). The entry function is the only symbol declared in the header; the static step functions are the C equivalent of private methods. The classic single-function form is still justified in freestanding or interrupt code, where stack depth and the absence of inlining make extra calls a real cost.
pitfalls: Omitting static gives a step function external linkage: it joins the program-wide namespace, can collide with same-named helpers from other translation units, and can be called by anyone.
A static function defined in a header produces one private copy per translation unit, so 'the same' step silently diverges between files (internal linkage is per translation unit).
There is no this: every step takes the receiver explicitly and repeats the error convention, so a long sequence turns into parameter plumbing that hides the purpose of the call list.
